en: Victorious are those showers of spray from the flowing fountain of the nectar of faith belonging to those who possess a special devotion to the Jina;
for even the collection of flowers and such, though insentient, attains as it were a proper sentience in the act of worshipping the worshipful.
In the past, at Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, the Jina was seated in solitude;
Anāthapiṇḍada approached and addressed the Blessed One.
O Blessed One, my daughter Sumāgadhā has reached maturity; she is renowned for her highly precious virtues and is like devotion to you, which is celebrated everywhere.
In the city of Puṇḍravardhana, belonging to the illustrious Sārthanātha, there is a son named Vṛṣabhadatta; he is desired as her husband.
“O Blessed One, if you so deem it right, I shall give that maiden to him;
for my wealth and life are subject to you, and I am indeed one who takes refuge in your command.”
When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One, whose intention was pure with affection, said:
"What harm is there? Let the daughter be given to him."
Having respectfully accepted the Teacher’s instruction and having prostrated before him,
the illustrious Anāthapiṇḍada departed for his own residence.
Then, bestowing abundant jewels and garments, he gave the maiden Sumāgadhā to that worthy suitor with magnificent splendor.
Then, as Sumāgadhā was being sent to a very distant land,
her eyes filled with tears through the recollection of the Blessed One’s feet.
After some time, having reached the city of Puṇḍravardhana,
she lived constantly in her husband's house, devoted to serving him.
Then once, her mother-in-law named Dhanavatī, who was intent on spending beyond measure, spoke to her while she was preparing the provisions for a feast.
"O Sumāgadhā, prepare all the requisites for worship!
The Jina, whose qualities are honored by the world, will come to our home tomorrow morning."
Those teachers, worthy of honor and objects of veneration for all people,
will arrive— monks intent on destroying delusion.
Having been addressed thus by her, she there became intent upon the undertaking,
perceiving that the worship had been prepared for the community of monks.
Then on another day, naked mendicants entered the house;
they had plucked out their hair and beards, and were sharpened by the hardships of their vows.
Seeing them shameless and unclothed, Sumāgadhā looked upon them like buffaloes fattened on the habit of eating beans and young grass.
Ashamed, she covered her face with her garment in the presence of her elders;
bowed down by exhaustion and despondency, she addressed her mother-in-law.
Ah, how wonderful that this custom has been observed after so long a time—
that here the womenfolk stand even before those who are naked!
"These untrained oxen, deprived of their horns, eat in your house;
surely the women do not feel shame before them because they are not human."
Your devotion is misplaced; what is this unrestrained course of action?
How can one who has not yet renounced food give up his clothing?

By the very act of plucking out his hair, he has manifested sharp cruelty; by the abandonment of even a loincloth, what talk can there be of virtuous conduct toward a good person? And in a face made terrifying by the onset of hypocrisy, anger itself is plainly visible.
Of these self-restrained ones, who are naked and seeking food like sacrificial animals.
Where these very animals are to be worshipped, who are there to be driven away?
Or rather, this is a defect of the region; it is a state of mind that merely follows the crowd.
To her who was speaking thus, her despondent mother-in-law replied:
"O blessed one, tell me, what kind of worship is performed in your father's house?"
"Listen, in my father's house the Blessed Jina is worshipped;
out of compassion for all the world, he is intent upon the excellence of virtue."
Dependent on meditation, with steady eyes, he is a full ocean of loveliness;
he bears a broad and straight bridge-like bridge of the nose,
and is beautiful with dangling ear-lobes that are radiant and devoid of ornaments.
By her very splendor, she spreads an indescribable peace within the hearts of the wise.
Upon his head is a crest-jewel consisting of a profusion of innate light;
his arms, possessing the luster of gold, are shaped like the trunks of lordly elephants;
and upon the palms of his hands are the lines of the conch, the banner, the lotus, and the garland.
He bears the mark befitting the great sovereignty of tranquility.
The very nature of those great sages, who produce desire in others yet are themselves devoid of all conceptualization of desire,
is such that the lower lip of a woman— who is the locus of passion, whose ground of memory is entirely exhausted, and who is utterly free from lust— is far more passionate than they.
His physical form is beloved by intense union; his friendship dwells within his mind;
his forbearance makes him one with that [virtue]; and compassion embraces his heart deeply.
This is observed in him who is devoted to the Earth, the ornament of all hopes.
The tranquility of that unprecedented jewel is of peerless majesty and is imbued with dispassion.
He is worthy of worship in our home, for by his renunciation the minds of the virtuous attain the state of being unencumbered by the silken garments of moral conduct.
By the mere remembrance of him, the universal protective gem,
living beings are no longer tormented by the serpent of worldly existence, whose fierce fangs are passion and hatred.
Having heard these words of hers, which were like nectar to her ears, her mother-in-law,
immediately brightened by her favor, spoke to her with great joy.
"O lady of lovely countenance, is there some means to behold him?
Might we too, through our connection with your merit, attain the abode of immortality?"
Thus entreated by her mother-in-law with gentle persuasion and a respectful mind, she, who considered herself devoted, spoke: "I shall show him to you."
Desiring to fulfill the burden of the equipment for her great vow,
she, mounted upon the scales of doubt, became for a moment intent on meditation.
Then, having ascended the palace and bowed toward the direction frequented by the Blessed One,
he offered a handful of flowers worthy of worship to the one deserving of worship.
Having performed worship with flowers, incense, and water, she, facing toward his feet,
spoke with her wide eyes overflowing with tears of joy.
"Out of compassion alone, O Blessed One, I— who am bereft of the Three Jewels—
have come to this distant land like a doe from your hermitage."
O Compassionate One, touch with Your glance me who have taken refuge at Your pair of lotus feet, even though I stand afar;
for the compassion of the great, whose minds are tender with affection, does not diminish toward those made distant by exile.
"O Blessed One, you have been invited today by me, the daughter of a slave;
O Lord, grant me the honor of your arrival tomorrow morning."
Having spoken thus, that garland of variegated flowers, released by her,
went through the sky like a messenger of devotion endowed with life.
That row of white, red, green, and black flowers, variegated by the smoke of incense as it drifted slowly through the sky,
shone for a long time like a young cloud clinging to Indra, resembling a flickering, trembling creeper.
Then, having reached Jetavana in an instant, Kusumāvalī,
full of devotion for the Teacher, fell at his lotus-like feet.
The Blessed One, the omniscient one, having understood everything desired,
spoke out of compassion to Ānanda in the presence of Sumāgadhā.
"We must depart in the morning for the city of Puṇḍravardhana;
Sumāgadhā requests my worship along with that of the Saṅgha."
Beyond this point, one must travel sixty-one hundred yojanas in a single day; no delay is appropriate here.
"Whosoever is powerful enough to travel through the sky by means of great supernatural power—
to each of them you must present an invitation slip."
Urged by the Sugata, he announced to the monks an invitation by means of voting-slips (śalākā) that was to be reached by traveling for one day.
When the voting sticks had been taken by all those of great supernatural power,
the Elder Pūrṇa also took his turn and drew the stick from the jar.
When the lot was drawn by that power he had attained, Ānanda, his face bright with a slight smile, said to him: "In whose hand [is it]? (KAvk 93.49)
One should not go even two steps toward the house of Anāthapiṇḍada;
it is surpassed by [the distance of] one hundred and sixty yojanas in just half a day.
Thus addressed by him, the elder, his face bowed with embarrassment, thought:
"Indeed, being inferior in the presence of one's own group is unbearable."

The afflictions, birth, old age, and so forth, accumulated since beginningless time, can be destroyed by one's adversaries; how much more so can the state of supernatural power (ṛddhipāda) be attained?
As he was reflecting thus with a mind of intense spiritual urgency,
a great supernatural power appeared in an instant to that one of pure heart.
Then, when the night had passed and at dawn, all the monks traveled through the sky in celestial palaces,
wearing the various garbs of the gods.
In the meantime, at her husband’s house, which was filled with preparations for a grand undertaking, Sumāgadhā was eager for a vision of the Blessed One.
Having ascended the palace together with her mother-in-law, father-in-law, and husband,
she stood there intent on preparing and collecting flowers, incense, and offerings.
Then the monk Ājñātakauṇḍinya,
mounted upon a horse-chariot and displaying various wonders of divine supernatural power, appeared for the first time.
Seeing him, who was radiant like the sun, her father-in-law and the others were struck with wonder and affectionately asked Sumāgadhā, "Who is this Blessed One?"
The Blessed One said: "This one who appears with the radiance of the sun is not seen;
this is the monk Ājñātakauṇḍinya, whose splendor remains undiminished."
Then, as the chariots arrived in succession, her father-in-law and the others said to her, "O blessed lady, who is this? Who is this? Is it the Blessed One?"
She said: "This is not the Teacher;
these are his disciples, worthy of his instruction—monks praiseworthy for their tranquility and blazing with the radiance of asceticism."
This glorious monk Mahākāśyapa— who approaches from afar, mounted upon a mountain peak beautiful with lovely golden trees— is like a wondrous power incarnate.
He who, mounted upon a five-faced chariot, approaches through the sky with a voice as deep as a water-laden cloud,
praised for his virtues— he is this very monk Śāriputra on earth.
He who, possessing infinite splendor, comes upon an elephant as white as Mount Kailāsa with four tusks—
the one who arrives in this world for the sake of the meritorious— is this very monk named Maudgalyāyana.
He who, having ascended a golden lotus with a stem of beryl and rich with filaments of jeweled sprouts,
approaches filling the quarters with his fragrance— he is this celebrated monk Aniruddha.
And he who, mounted upon Garuḍa, plunges into the highest reaches of the sky, dispersing the clouds with the wind from his wings—
this is that full monk Pūrṇa, the son of Maitrāyaṇī, who traverses the vast forest.

Having established himself in the infinitely peaceful path beyond envy, this powerful monk, a great ocean of being, moves about satisfying the quarters with the nectar of his radiance; he is the conqueror of the future.
Having climbed the vast golden palm tree, which is delightful with its encircling, swaying creepers,
he who approaches with the splendor of one filled with merit is this wise monk Upāli.
Having ascended the peak of a Vaiḍūrya palace, its leaf-patterns radiant with gold and jewels,
he who approaches as if anointing all with his splendors— he is this very monk named Kātyāyana.

This is the monk Kauṣṭhila, of most profound intellect, who, having mounted his bull as if it were the personified Dharma, traverses the sky; he is the support for those firmly established in their foundations.
Making the sky momentarily beautiful with waves of smiles and the splendor of celestial swans,
here approaches that monk named Pilindavatsa, a treasure-house of asceticism.
He who approaches, dwelling amidst the interior of a forest where canopies of flowering creepers are spread,
is that monk Śroṇakoṭi, renowned for his unimpaired splendor and his indifference toward home.
He who shines in heaven as a universal monarch is this very son of the Teacher named Rāhula;
adorned with a golden luster that illuminates the quarters of space, he appears like Mount Meru in another form.
From the mountains, from the ends of the quarters, from the circle of the earth, and from the depths of the sky’s expanse,
these countless and wondrous assemblies of monks arrive, seated upon various jeweled thrones and vehicles.
As she related this in due order, they beheld the community of monks turning away;
then, filled with joy, wonder, and agitation, they simultaneously came under the sway of that peerless splendor.
Then the world, possessing the color of glowing gold dust, became as radiant as a hundred suns;
yet, through the complete pacification of all distress, it was as cool as a hundred garlands of moonbeams.
Then the Lord of Jinas, accompanied by a retinue of immortals led by Dhanapati, Śakra, and Brahmā on their vast journey through the sky,
came within the range of vision of those possessing merit, appearing amidst the splendor of flowers scattered by the women of the city of the gods.
Having entered that city, which possessed eighteen gateways and was like his own eighteen-fold form, he, who is of eighteen manifestations,
constructed for Sumāgadhā a palace composed of moonstone jewels and radiant peaks.
Having prostrated there with all kinds of abundant offerings,
the citizens worshipped him from every side, both outside and reflected upon the walls.
Having accepted the worship out of compassion for Sumāgadhā, the compassionate Blessed One, together with his Saṅgha,
bestowed grace upon all the lineages through his benevolent glances and distribution of gifts.
Sumāgadhā, together with her circle of parents-in-law and all the other citizens,
became pure in intention through that teaching of the Teacher, having realized the Truth at that very moment.
Having observed the vast power of the merit resulting from Sumāgadhā’s wholesome deeds,
those monks, out of curiosity, questioned the delightful Jina regarding her original history.
Questioned by them in the assembly regarding the cause of Sumāgadhā’s welfare,
the All-Seeing Blessed One spoke, illuminating the faces of the quarters with the radiance of his teeth.
Formerly, in Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Kṛki;
he had a daughter named Kāñcanamālā, who wore a golden garland upon her breasts.
Constantly devoted to the Teacher named Kāśyapa,
she performed service for him together with five hundred female companions.
Once, due to the sight of a portentous dream, that lord of men,
agitated by fear and doubt, questioned those skilled in interpreting omens.
Out of hatred for the princess, those who knew omens said to him:
"By offering the heart of one who is exceedingly dear into the fire, one attains auspiciousness."
Thus, disregarding their exceedingly cruel words,
the king went to see the venerable Kāśyapa at the urging of his daughter.
Having approached him, he said: "O Omniscient One, today I have seen a most extraordinary dream; you ought to tell me its entire result."
As I was going out through the window, I saw an elephant with its tail tucked in;
likewise, as I ran behind, I saw a well for one who was thirsty.
He was satisfied with a measure of barley meal, yet he sold a measure of pearls;
pieces of wretched wood were seen being equated in value with sandalwood.
Just as a great elephant, its limbs smeared with filth, is challenged by a young elephant in battle, so too did that monkey, his body covered in impurities, rush forward, smearing his enemies.
And the monkey, consecrated over a vast kingdom and a treasury of mischievous gestures,
was like a cloth pulled by eighteen men that could not be exhausted.
Even beautiful groves of flowers and fruits were plundered by thieves,
and the vast multitude of people became addicted to hatred, derision, and quarreling.
"I consider the fruit of these wondrous dreams to be most terrible.
Thus questioned by the king, the Blessed Kāśyapa replied:
When the lifespan of people is one hundred years, the Teacher, the peaceful Śākyamuni, the Victor, will appear as an ocean of nectar; that elephant was seen by you.
In his later time as well, his disciples, relying on the Kali age,
will abandon their moral discipline, virtuous qualities, and proper conduct, becoming full of corruption.
By force, those who dwell in households— whose discernment is immature and slight—
will themselves adopt service and indeed perform the teaching.
Since he runs after services as one who seeks gain,
he looks back like a thirsty man who, while walking, gazes at a well behind him.
Blinded by greed and struck down by delusion,
they will commit the supreme act of selling a prastha of the pearls of the factors of enlightenment for a prastha of barley meal.

Out of their ignorance, those who fail to distinguish between them will, through delusion, attempt to equate the wretched wood of the words of the heretics with the sandalwood of the Buddha’s teachings.
In some places, having encountered a well-behaved and disciplined elephant among monks,
a monk who is but a young elephant of immoral conduct will treat him with contempt out of rivalry.
With his limbs smeared with impurities from his fickleness, this monkey-monk,
by anointing others with his own faults, will make them resemble himself.
And the consecration of Ṣaṇḍaka shall be like that of a monkey;
yet the cloth of the Perfect Buddha’s teaching, though being dragged about, will not perish.
They will even act as thieves toward the property of the Saṅgha and the fruit-bearing groves;
they will be prone to mutual quarreling and will be full of slander.
"Upon the conclusion of the ripening of your dream, these fruits shall appear upon the ground";
hearing these words of the Teacher, the lord of the earth was filled with wonder.
Then that Teacher, having given a discourse on the Dharma to the king along with his followers,
prescribed for Kāñcanamālā the virtues leading to arhatship.
In another birth, she made an offering at a stupa with a garland of oranges;
by that very merit, she was born marked with a golden garland.
By the exceedingly great power of her merit,
this Sumāgadhā has today become a perfect bridge of virtue for the multitude of people.
Having thus addressed them, the Blessed One, the Conqueror, traveled through the sky together with the monks to the Jeta Grove, filling the quarters with his radiance.

For men, there is a powerful and yet utterly false longing for a son for the sake of the prosperity of their lineage; yet if that son is devoid of virtue, then that lineage is as good as lost. Indeed, it is through the power of merit that such a virtuous daughter is born.
In the lord of the great river of saṃsāra, the pair of lineages is indeed carried across like two boats.
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter, the *Sumāgadhā-avadāna*, in the *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* composed by Kṣemendra.
